criterion_notes.c1: Examines community rural drinking-water service access via the functionality and durability of 5,921 improved rural water points across 15 districts in Tanzania.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this paper would be included because alongside water-point technology and age it empirically tests three community-level O&M management indicators (whether meetings were held, whether income was collected, and whether O&M expenditure was made in the year prior to the survey). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met: the study does not examine any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as tariff or cost-recovery rules, institutional/utility ownership or management model variation, eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, discretion, or regulatory enforcement). Although the WPM questionnaire recorded 'institution in charge of the management', institutional type is never analysed in Results; the authors explicitly note that 'the governance structure is the same for all regions' (p. 6), that the binary income item does not capture tariff or fund-use rules ('the data do not tell us whether this money was to be used for reconstruction, as an initial contribution for another WP, or for other purposes', p. 4), and discuss the 1991 National Water Policy shift only as unanalysed macro-governance historical background (p. 7).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative cross-sectional study analysing Water Point Mapping (WPM) survey data collected in 2005-2006 across 5,921 improved water points (5,852 with construction year) using Pearson's chi-square tests and linear regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports water-point functionality (whether an improved water point yields water regularly and is used on a day-to-day basis) across districts, technologies, and years since installation—a direct measure of community water service availability and reliability.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (5,921 improved community rural water points in 15 rural districts of Tanzania covering 15% of the rural population), exposures (water-point technology category, years since construction, and binary prior-year O&M meetings/income/expenditure indicators), outcome (water-point functionality), and study design (cross-sectional Water Point Mapping survey) are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: The aim of the study is to establish the relationships between technology, functionality and durability of rural water points, based on the review of WPM data from 5,921 improved water points. Data were collected between 2005 and 2006 by Wateraid.
One water point (WP) is considered to be functional if it yields water regularly and is being used by people as a water source on a day to day basis.
Hence, the sample that was used is of 5,921 water points. From those, 5,852 contain the information of the year of construction. These are used for the analysis of functionality over time.

Income was reported to be slightly above 50% for functional WPs but 43% for non-functional ones. Only 35.3% of functional WPs and 17.1% of not functional WPs reported expenditures for the year prior to the survey.
Since the governance structure is the same for all regions, we analysed the relationship with general poverty indicators.

raw_response.exposure: Water-point technology category (handpumps, motorised pumping systems, gravity-fed systems, others), years since construction, and generic community O&M activity indicators (whether meetings were held, income was collected, and expenditure was made in the previous year)
raw_response.outcome: Functionality of improved rural water points (yielding water regularly and used on a day-to-day basis) and functionality decay rates over time
raw_response.population_and_sample: 5,921 improved rural community water points (5,852 with year of construction) surveyed across 15 rural districts of Tanzania covering 15% of the national rural population (unit of analysis: water point, aggregated to district and regional levels)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. While the study empirically examines rural drinking-water point functionality across 5,921 water points in Tanzania (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6) and passes the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 via community O&M management indicators (whether meetings were held and whether any income or expenditure occurred in the prior year), it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing access (such as tariff or cost-recovery rules, utility/institutional ownership variation, eligibility or documentation requirements, administrative burden, or enforcement). Governance structure is uniform across the regions studied and national policy history is discussed only as unanalysed background.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational survey (Water Point Mapping census across 15 rural districts)
